claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar-colony microstructure produced by conventional processing.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar boundaries produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure during room-temperature tension.
Post-forging annealing at 550–650°C will relax residual stresses at the lamellar interfaces.
Post-forging annealing at 550–650°C will trigger coherent nanometer-scale precipitates along the lamellar interfaces.
The coherent nanoscale precipitates will facilitate dislocation transmission across lamellar boundaries.
Facilitated dislocation transmission will suppress dislocation pile-ups at the lamellar boundaries.
Suppressing dislocation accumulation and associated local stress concentrations will reduce microcracking and brittle fracture.
The nanoscale precipitates will contribute to strength through precipitation hardening.
The annealed alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile strain to failure than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
A fine lamellar eutectic HEA architecture can combine high fracture strength with high ductility.
Coherent lamellar boundaries can permit planar dislocation slip across interfaces, and lamellar shearing can accommodate large local strain rather than forming a crack.
The proposed treatment is intended for eutectic HEAs with dual-phase lamellar microstructures tested in room-temperature tension.
The treatment may not be effective for substantially different microstructures or non-ambient operating temperatures.
The optimal annealing duration, precipitate-distribution uniformity, and balance between strengthening and possible embrittlement are undetermined.
